speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: RESIGNATION FROM GOVERNMENT OF HON. PAUL HELLYER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house that I have this morning received a letter of resignation as a member of the government from the Hon. Paul Hellyer, Minister of Transport, and that I have recommended to the Deputy Governor General, the Right Hon. Mr. Justice Cartwright, that the minister's resignation be accepted.
I will table later in the day correspondence exchanged between the minister and myself relative to the resignation.

Order, please. I have a bit of a difficult problem which I have to bring to the attention of the house, in that earlier today the Chair received two notices provided for under Standing Order 26. One of the two motions preceded the other, and I might say had the additional qualification of having been tendered and received within the time limit set by the rules. In fairness, and in
attempting to consider this matter as Solomon might have, I think that the first motion, the one received initially by the Chair, should be put, subject to the Chair reading both motions to the house. maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 HOUSING RESIGNATION OF MINISTER AND FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ADEQUATE ACCOMMODATION-MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), to move the adjournment of the house under Standing Order 26, for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the resignation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), because of the failure of the government to agree to take action to increase the housing supply in Canada, and the consequent danger of further delay in the taking of adequate legislative and financial steps to meet the housing crisis that now faces this country.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 HOUSING RESIGNATION OF MINISTER AND FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ADEQUATE ACCOMMODATION-MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
As I indicated a moment ago, I had received the motion which has now been read by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and a similar motion from the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) moving the adjournment of the house under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the resignation from the government of the Hon. Paul Hellyer as Minister of Transport, because of the failure of the government to reach decisions urgently needed to meet the housing crisis in Canada.
Since both notices cover exactly the same ground I might deal with both motions at the same time. The matter raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands and the proposed motion by the Leader of the Opposition deal of course with a most important matter, so important indeed that there is some thought in my mind that it should be considered by the house as soon as possible. As hon. members know, the house, under a special order, has set aside two days sittings for a discussion of Canada's participation in NATO.

Resignation of Minister of Transport
I am of the opinion that it would not be desirable to alter our business for today. Whether the business for tomorrow should be altered is another matter to which I have given serious thought. In reviewing the request for adjournment of the house I have had difficulty in resolving the question of whether this matter should or might be raised in another form. It seems to me the matter of housing is in the circumstances a continuing problem but to that problem has been added another, the resignation of the Minister of the Crown who has been charged with the federal government's responsibility in the field of housing. The resignation of the minister is not necessarily in itself reason or ground for moving the adjournment of the house nor is the operation of the government's housing policy necessarily a matter of such urgent importance as to warrant a motion under Standing Order 26.
Having said that, however, when these two events are tied together it seems to the Chair there is a matter of urgency which may very well satisfy the provisions of Standing Order 26 in respect of the matter of urgency of debate. Having put aside any doubt in respect of the question of raising this matter as a matter of confidence in the government under Standing Order 58, I am inclined to allow the motion under the discretion vested in the Chair by citation (9) of Standing Order 26. I have said that I do not believe the business of the house for today should be disturbed, in view of the special order setting aside today for the consideration of government policy dealing with NATO. Any decision under Standing Order 26 would apply to tomorrow rather than today.
In view of the desirability of resolving certain procedural questions in relation to Bill C-150 I am directing that the matter be set down for consideration at two o'clock tomorrow afternoon provided the procedural matters relating to Bill C-150 have been disposed of earlier.

speechtext:

We have a motion before the house in very clear terms, and the Leader of the Opposition has done nothing but condemn the government for its statement. The subamendment offered by the New Democratic party does some condemning too, but at least it also makes some positive suggestions. The problem with their amendment, however, is one which appears to haunt that party. It is based not on the world as it is but on a world that they would like to think exists. But the government is in a position of responsibility 29180-500J

and it has to deal with the world as it is. Canada and Canadians have to operate in a world that is much more dangerous and complex than members of the New Democratic party would lead us to believe.
The Leader of the Opposition has developed a complicated line of reasoning to suggest that in some way the government has determined upon its defence policy before settling upon its foreign policy. The superficiality of this argument becomes obvious when we consider the circumstances under which we are having this debate.
The government felt under an obligation, and certainly as Secretary of State for External Affairs I urged this upon the government, to give to our NATO allies as much information as we could about our future position before the Washington meeting of our NATO friends. It would have been very simple for the government to limit its announcement, in contemplation of that meeting, to its decision to remain in NATO. That would have been the simplest thing to do. It would have avoided the kind of debate we are having now. We could have avoided any mention of our decision to reduce, in due course and in an orderly way, the size of our forces on the ground in Europe.
I can well imagine the accusations that could properly have been made against the government if we had simply announced our intention to stay in the alliance prior to that meeting, and then later let people in on the fact that we intended to reduce our forces in Europe. That would have been dishonest. That would have been concealing. We felt that the only frank and honest thing we could do was to convey to our allies, first, our foreign policy decision to stay in the alliance and, second, our military decision, still incomplete, to reduce our forces in Europe. I say that this decision is still incomplete since it cannot in the nature of things be completed, and it was impossible for the government to have gone any further at that stage than to make the decision it made on April 3. I say to the Leader of the Opposition who made so much of this argument, who said the government's statement was deliberately intended to mean different things to different people, that it would have been quite impossible for us, in advance of our consultation with our allies, to have gone any further than we did at that stage.
As I say, we had an alternative. We could have said nothing. Then we could have been charged with deceit. As it is, I suggest to the

April 24, 1969

Leader of the Opposition that we are being as frank and honest as it was possible for us to have been under the circumstances.
We said that the planned and phased reduction in our forces in Europe will be made in consultation with our allies. We have not undertaken to consult our allies on whether or not we should reduce our forces in Europe. This decision has been made by the government and is not, as such, negotiable. However, we will be consulting our allies about how this decision is to be put into effect. This is no more than the responsible behavior to be expected of this country.
The other NATO nations may wish to make adjustments arising from Canadian reductions in strength in Europe, and we will certainly want to carry out our plans1 causing the least possible difficulty to our allies who are also, it should be remembered, among our oldest and closest friends in the international community. As a matter of fact, under cross-examination at a press conference in Washington I said it was not our intention by our action to weaken the alliance, and that remains1 the policy of Canada.
Without attempting any general definition, let me make even more clear what we mean by consultation in these circumstances. As we work out how we are going to make the planned and phased reduction of our forces in Europe we will keep our allies informed, listen to their views, and discuss the matter with them. The problems they face, and the views they express, will be taken into account in our decision-making process, but eventually the decision can only be made by the Canadian government, having regard to our national interests, our capacities and our objectives.

The fact that the decision-making process with regard to our military presence in Europe is still going on while the basic decision to stay in NATO could be announced on April 3 shows clearly how defence policy flows from foreign policy. We had to assess the importance to us of our membership in the alliance having regard to our other responsibilities and areas of interest. We had to make our own judgment of the usefulness of NATO to us as a means through which we can contribute to international stability and as an important element in our relations with Europe. We had to study NATO's capacity as an instrument for increasing contacts and improving relations with the U.S.S.R. and its associate states. These are by no means all of foreign policy considerations that went into our review of our place in NATO, but they are among the more important. It was only after we had dealt with all these and other foreign policy questions that we could turn our minds to the effect of our political decision upon our defence arrangements.

Evolution, change, unpredictability-in this world situation Canada must be in a position to adapt its policies and its outlook quickly, flexibly and effectively to the challenges of the future. We must not isolate ourselves in the problems of the past.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Calgary Centre.

April 24, 1969

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) spent some time on what was bound to be an unsuccessful attempt to explain the unexplainable so far as the conflicts are concerned in what he, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and other ministers have said. In addition, he gave us a few generalities. The only definite point in his speech was that he made it plain that the consultation referred to in the motion means no more than telling our allies in NATO that our troops will be withdrawn and advising them to take the necessary steps to fill the gap. That is all the consultation amounts to. This is the one thing the Secretary of State for External Affairs did make clear.
The motion of the Prune Minister is in two parts. The first part states that Canada will remain in NATO. The second part states that we will withdraw from NATO our forces in Europe. It is quite evident that the two parts of the resolution are in direct contradiction of each other and therefore in essence the motion is a fraud.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
During the past year there has been almost complete confusion as to the government's intentions in respect of NATO. This has been the result of the conflicting statements of the Prime Minister and other ministers about what the government intended to do in so far as NATO was concerned. The present motion and the Prime Minister's statement and explanation of it continue this confusion. We now know definitely that it is the intention of the government to remove a number of our troops from Europe. As pointed out yesterday by my leader, we do not know whether a few or practically all our forces in Europe will be withdrawn. The confusion still exists and we are still up in the air in this regard.
We must consider the whole matter in conjunction with the Prime Minister's earlier statements, both before he occupied his present position and since. For the most part these statements, particularly some of his earlier ones, were definitely along the line that Canada should withdraw its forces from NATO. Thus the only conclusion I can come to is that the Prime Minister intends to end our military contributions as quickly as possible.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
An hon. member opposite applauds. There is no doubt that his attitude is shared by a few members but not by the
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
majority in this chamber, including many on the Liberal side.
Let me put this another way. The Prime Minister's policy is one of scuttle-get out just as fast as possible. This is the same policy General de Gaulle followed. The only conclusion one can come to is that the Prime Minister is using General de Gaulle as an example in this regard and intends to do exactly the same thing, with perhaps one difference in that he intends to do so in slower stages. The final result will be the same.
Yesterday the Prime Minister in effect accused those of us who do not agree with his views in respect of NATO of living in the past. As recorded at page 7867 of Hansard he said:
Canadians must be prepared to face the world of actuality, the world of 1969.
That is exactly what the Prime Minister is not doing. Ke does not recognize that the basic threat to our security which brought NATO into existence in the first place still exists and that we have a responsibility to continue to play a role commensurate with our population and resources to counter that threat.
A great deal of wishful thinking has taken place in the last few years along the lines that the aggressive intention of Russia has disappeared and that a period of detente has occurred. Some people believe that all that is necessary is to treat Russia with kid gloves and in a nice way and this detente will continue. The events in Czechoslovakia last year ended these illusions very abruptly for most people. It did not end them for everybody. These events ended the hopes of those people in Europe who are under a direct threat. This was made abundantly clear to the members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence who spent two weeks in Europe immediately before Easter. This was the reaction we observed in every country we visited, whether a NATO country or a neutral country such as Switzerland or Sweden.
Let me point out that the first object of the foreign and defence policy of any country is to maintain its security and independence. In the past many countries were able to do this on their own; however, that time has long passed. Security and independence can only be maintained now by most countries, particularly countries of our size, and I have in mind population, through alliances with like-minded nations. These people face the same
April 24, 1S69

dangers and must combine to resist these dangers.
The most important of these alliances to our security during the past 20 years has been NATO. The purpose of that alliance throughout its existence has been the maintenance of peace and to prevent a third great war rather than having to fight such a war. This deterrent role of the alliance must be emphasized and re-emphasized because many people still think of NATO as an organization designed to fight a war rather than to prevent one. The alliance has prevented a major war or further aggression in Europe during the past 20 years. It can continue to do so only if it remains strong, and it will only remain strong if its members continue to contribute military forces relative to their ability to do so.
This is the very thing the present government through this motion is proposing to end. We will not contribute military forces to the alliance with any relationship to our ability, population and resources to do so. We will not be contributing forces in relation to any other factor. I am sure everyone will agree that France's withdrawal of its troops from the NATO alliance seriously weakened it. The result has been that other countries have had to increase their contribution to make up for the loss of French forces. Surely no one would attempt to argue that the withdrawal of Canadian forces from NATO will not further weaken the alliance.
While it is true that our forces are relatively small in numbers, they are very highly trained and very efficient, probably more so than any others in Europe. This again was made plain to us during our trip overseas. The withdrawal of Canadian forces will create a gap which will be hard to fill. This was also impressed upon us by the people in Europe.
More important than the military loss as a result of the withdrawal of Canadian troops is the psychological effect and the feeling it will produce in European countries. They will begin to feel that we are retreating to the American fortress and that they cannot count on us to give them help in the event of war. This is bound to result in a decline in morale and the feeling that perhaps the other small members of the alliance should do the same thing.
The Prime Minister has discounted the so-called domino theory that because one country takes a certain line of action others are likely to follow. The theory is that because a

country such as Canada withdraws from NATO other European countries are likely to do the same thing. That may be his opinion and the opinion of some members of the committee, but it was not the opinion of one single individual we talked with in Europe. The European people were unanimous, including those in neutral countries such as Sweden and Switzerland, that a Canadian withdrawal of troops from NATO would weaken the alliance and have the effect of increasing this already existing feeling in the small European countries, with the result that they might follow Canada's example and do likewise. Therefore we must keep in mind the psychological effect from both these factors, that of perhaps inducing other people to follow the same course, and that of making the Europeans feel they are more isolated and cannot count on our help. These psychological effects will be very serious indeed.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The Prime Minister stated, as recorded on page 7869 of Hansard:
The government's NATO decision is based on the belief that, during the forthcoming years, there are better uses of the Canadian forces-
I ask the Prime Minister and every other member of the house, what better uses are there for Canadian forces than their use in NATO? How can they contribute more to Canada's security than by the role they are playing in NATO at the present time? I have given this question considerable thought, and I think I have some knowledge and experience in these matters. I can think of no single way, not one, in which Canadian forces could do more for the security of this country, the maintenance of peace and the independence of this country than the role they are discharging in Europe at the present time.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
The various statements the Prime Minister has made, particularly in his speech in Calgary, have left the impression that nearly all of our military forces are devoted to NATO. This, of course, is very far from being the case; it is a complete distortion of the facts. We are supposed to have about 100,000 people in our forces, though we are admittedly not up to strength, and only about 10,000 of them are on NATO service in Europe or about one-tenth of our forces. It is true that our maritime forces have a NATO-commitment, it is true that we have other possible commitments to NATO from the forces in Canada; but the fact is that the

April 24, 1969

great bulk of our Canadian forces are not oriented to NATO or committed to NATO. The bulk of our forces are available for the other tasks the armed forces have to perform, the protection of the land, sea and air of our country, NORAD, peacekeeping missions, and so on. I object to the Prime Minister trying to convey the impression to the people of Canada that practically all our forces are devoted to NATO. This is just not so. Quite a small number of our forces proportionately are devoted to that end.
I repeat, in closing, what I said at the beginning of my remarks. The Prime Minister's policy is one of scuttle; it is a retreat to isolationism and continentalism, as stated by my leader yesterday and expressed in the amendment moved by this party, which I hope will receive the support of the house.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this NATO debate primarily because I am a member of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence and have been since the beginning of the 28th parliament. As such I have some strong views in this regard and I would like to express those views today in the House of Commons. Prior to doing so, may I say I think it is important that the House of Commons and the people of Canada realize the scope of the study made by the committee on this very important problem.
On Thursday, January 16, 1969, pursuant to an order issued by the House of Commons, our committee was given the obligation of looking into policy changes in defence and external affairs. Following this, we held 24 meetings in Canada and heard evidence pro and con from people with divergent views, ranging from getting completely out of NATO, to staying in and getting in much more deeply, or to becoming an unaligned, neutral country. Name it, and we heard about it in that committee. In Canada we received testimony from 16 witnesses, and between March 8 and March 22 we travelled to Europe in order to see for ourselves the role our forces were playing in Europe and to discuss these problems with leaders and representatives of other countries. We also looked into the possibilities of neutrality in Sweden, and peacekeeping operations in Cyprus.
I speak on this subject because I think it is important that we establish the scope and depth of the study given this matter by the committee. But there were also certain limitations, the primary limitation being time. We found ourselves faced with a fact that we
[Mr. Harkness.l
could not ignore, namely, the Washington NATO meeting on April 10, wherein the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) intended to outline broadly the conclusions of this policy review. We were forced, as a result, to come to conclusions prematurely. This is not to say that I back away from any of those conclusions; in fact, I support them very strongly. I did in the committee, and I do so here in the House of Commons.
The important thing is that defence and foreign affairs are not limited just to NATO. There is the whole problem of national defence, which takes in Canadian sovereignty, NORAD, peacekeeping and many other aspects of Defence. We must look at all avenues. Our committee, because of this limitation of time and our being forced to come to a conclusion by certain deadline, had to confine itself solely to our participation in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. We did not have enough time to hear evidence regarding all aspects even in regard to this limited question. I think every member of the committee would agree with this statement.
Our committee made a report which said that we could not make a recommendation in terms of role or numbers of forces in Europe, or whether we should be involved in a nuclear strike force or maintain a mechanized brigade. We could say nothing with regard to any of these matters. We felt that the matter was of sufficient importance that we as a committee, and the government, give these questions urgent consideration.
There is one element of our report that does not ring entirely true with the government's proposals. Recommendation No. 3 of the report said we should maintain our present role in Europe until such time as the major equipment of our mechanized brigade and air role in Europe was phased out and became obsolete. We made that recommendation in good faith. I think we felt it was quite important. But I am the first to admit that because I did not study the nature of this whole matter there is reason to question even one's own decision in this regard.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: You had lots of chance to study it.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: We did not study the question of role.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Why didn't you?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Because we did not have time. In any event, I would appreciate it if the hon.
April 24, 1969

member would be kind enough to save his interruptions for another speaker.
I would like to talk about the recommendations made by the committee. The first was that we remain in NATO. If you read the motion before the house today, you must come to the conclusion that this is exactly what the government wants to do.
In our second recommendation, which is a very important one and I think much of the controversy involves this question, we said that Canada should continue to maintain forces in Europe as a contribution to the collective defensive arrangements of NATO. I subscribe to this principle, the vast majority of the members of the committee subscribe to it and, in my interpretation of what the Prime Minister has said, he subscribes to it as well. In this regard I should like to quote the following from the motion:
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
-to take early steps to bring about a planned and phased reduction of the size of the Canadian forces in Europe.
A reduction is not a withdrawal. I do not think you can reduce the forces to nothing and still be honest with the terms of this motion.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Who said they were honest?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
I believe the Government said exactly what it means-a phased reduction. It is very important to know whether it is going to be reduced to such an extent that our contribution would become token and meaningless. I would be absolutely opposed to that now, and in the future on the basis of the information I now have. However, I do not think that that is the intent of this motion. I think that we are going to maintain our forces in Europe and we are going to play a role in the defence of the free world through our participation in the NATO alliance.
I will give a couple of arguments supporting my belief that it is extremely important that we maintain a physical presence1 in Europe. First of all I believe, on the basis of evidence, that the real threat to international peace lies in Europe. This is where the two superpowers have sufficient interest at stake that a nuclear war could occur. That is what the NATO alliance is all about, and I believe that is why we must remain a part of it.
The next point is that there is nothing more valuable for us as a parliament to do than to ensure that our government takes appropriate action to preserve peace and avoid a nuclear 29180-501

war. That is in the interest of every citizen, whether he has good or bad housing. Whatever his problem is I think he wants to live more than he desires some of these other things. The preservation of peace is the most important thing. Our job is to determine how we can best achieve this lofty objective. I believe it is very important that we maintain a presence in Europe in order to achieve that absolutely basic and essential objective.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Some may argue that we can rely upon the nuclear deterrent of the United States or upon the nuclear stalemate between the two superpowers. I say that this1 is not looking at the whole question, according to the evidence that I have heard from those who gave evidence and who spoke to us in Europe. The problem in Europe is to have a conventional force that would make the nuclear power of the U. S. credible.
If you withdrew all the conventional forces in NATO from Europe, you would do nothing more than to encourage Russia to expand its territory and dominate Europe completely. So we must do something to stop that. It is not reasonable to expect the United States to start a nuclear exchange with Russia, which would surely destroy both countries, in the event that Russia or the Warsaw Pact countries were to move forward a little bit in Europe. It is too monstrous to believe that any rational person would destroy his whole nation over such an issue. So to restrain them we must prove to Russia that we can respond in more than just a nuclear manner. We must have the conventional capacity to wage a conventional war in Europe in order to avoid a nuclear war. I think that that is part of the reason why our troops in Europe are necessary and important.
The third recommendation that we made in the committee regarding the long-term military role of Canada is consistent with phase two of the government's review. However, I would be very interested to find out what their conclusions will be, and I think we would all be interested in making this determination. I do not think you can predict from the resolution exactly what it means or where it leads. I believe the government intends to keep Canadian forces in Europe and to play a meaningful role there.
The fifth recommendation by the committee is in regard to the role played by Canada in NATO toward the achievement of a detente and balanced force reductions in Europe consistent with the Harmel report. I believe that

April 24. 1969

that is totally consistent with all the statements ever made by the Prime Minister with regard to our foreign affairs and defence policy.
In conclusion I should like to say that I oppose the amendment proposed by the Leader of Her Majesty's Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). I do so because I do not honestly and sincerely believe that the government through this motion is retreating into isolationism. There is ample evidence that the government, probably more than any other government that I know of, is doing exactly the reverse. For this reason I cannot support the amendment. Second, I cannot possibly support the amendment to the amendment proposed by the New Democratic party, which in effect calls for real isolationism and for a complete withdrawal from Europe. I do not think this is in the interests of Canada or of the free world. Third, so far as the Prime Minister's motion is concerned I wish to say that I am willing to support it and I do so without any reservation, trusting that we will in effect play a meaningful role in the preservation of peace in this country and in the world. We Canadians have more to lose from a nuclear war than most countries in Europe. We are between two superpowers and we must ensure that they do not engage in nuclear war. I am confident we will play a meaningful, viable and realistic role for peace in the world in which we live today.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) speak eloquently on the trip we made with the committee on external affairs and national defense, in conjunction with the review of Canada's role within NATO.
The hon. member for Ontario seems to have changed his mind quite a bit since that trip on which he was one of those who recommended most strongly to the committee that Canada should continue to keep forces in Europe to participate in NATO's joint defence agreements.
His speech this afternoon contradicts the remarks and claims he made to the committee to the effect that Canada should be allowed, as before, to keep troops overseas under its NATO commitments, and to play the role it should.
During the election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke to us of a policy of participation. I wonder if that was his
(Mr. Cafik.]
goal in advocating a review of Canada's foreign policy with regard to NATO, for we have heard several ministers say exactly the contrary to what 'they had formerly advocated in this house.
At this point, I should like to mention the statements made in this house by the Minister of Communications (Mr. KieransO, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), and especially the firm and categorical assertions of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux), who repeatedly stated that Canada should stay in NATO and continue in the role it has played for 20 years.
I wonder whether the involved and timid statement of the Prime Minister on the role Canada should now play within NATO and on the reduction of its forces may not have had as sole purpose to save the face of the cabinet and tone down the differences of opinions within the cabinet and amongst government members.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, there were 17 Liberal members accompanying the delegation on the visits we made across Europe in the course of that trip. I may be mistaken but there were at least 14 of them who shared the opinion now expressed by the opposition, which is that Canada should remain in NATO, take time before reducing its forces and prevent its foreign policy from getting bogged in isolationism and con-tinentalism.
Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of National Defence has, so far, tempered his statements about the position adopted by the cabinet and the Prime Minister, it is due to the fact that he is a very patient man. I am convinced that he shares* the opinion of the opposition and whenever he feels he should state that our role within NATO should be maintained in order to preserve world peace and to sustain the prestige of Canada among the concert of nations, he will always win the admiration and support of the members on this side of the house.
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Ontario said earlier, we have indeed visited many countries, including England where we met the Minister of Defence and the Foreign Secretary.
We also have been to Geneva where we met with Mr. Ignatieff, Canada's representative on the disarmament Commission, who said, it substance, that he did not believe that Canada would decide to review its role within NATO with the purpose of curtailing its military forces since by so doing Canada would
April 24. 1969

jeopardize its prestige in the eyes of the Disarmament Commission of which it is now a member.
As I said a short while ago, we met the Defence Minister and the Foreign Secretary of Great Britain. Even if that country has already reduced its armed forces within NATO, we were asked not to follow suit because this would have dire results for the future of the Alliance.
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that all the people that we met were wrong all at the same time. The Prime Minister and the cabinet surely cannot convince us that they are the only ones to be right when Canada's role within NATO is under review.
We also visited a neutral country, Sweden, and we know how much this country is spending for national defence in an effort to safeguard its neutrality. We were told that should that country be attacked, it would still go to NATO to find protection for the national territory.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe that all those experienced people who live in those circles, who have been dealing with NATO for 20 years, who keep in touch with defence experts, have been backing the wrong horse. I would rather support the argument of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) to the effect that we should stay within NATO as long as international relations are as tense as they are now.
The Prime Minister said in his speech that he was charged with having made a premature announcement, and, in my estimation, it was.
If we consider what happened recently in Czchoslovakia, we realize that Russia and its satellites have concentrated in Europe considerable forces of an extraordinary mobility that startled our allies. When it invaded Czechoslovakia, Russia initiated an international crisis. Had NATO, a deterrent force, not existed, we can wonder if the Russians would not have invaded Berlin, thus launching another world war.
In my view, that is the reason for the existence of NATO. In twenty years of existence, because of its deterrent capacity, its efforts to reduce international tension and its strength of which it convinced the enemy, the organization was successful in avoiding major and minor conflicts. At present, its role and its existence are still justified, if we do not want another world war to happen.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, I strongly support the amendment moved by the Leader of 29180-50U

the Opposition, because I am convinced that it is still the best policy Canada could follow in 1969.
Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker for the Conservative party, the former Minister of National Defence, stated the reasons why we should not withdraw from NATO nor, least of all, reduce our forces.
It is obvious-and all the experts we met during our trip said so quite clearly-that should Canada decide to reduce its forces serving under NATO, it would create some kind of psychosis in the other member countries. It would weaken the morale of those countries which might then be inclined to follow the example of Canada as far as its foreign policy is concerned.
The decision of the present government will contribute shortly to the disintegration of NATO and it will also encourage some NATO members, as I was saying a moment ago, to follow the example of Canada and to reduce their forces.
The government's decision aimed at reducing its forces within NATO is going to diminish the prestige of Canada within international organizations, above all as far as disarmament and detente are concerned in the world.
How shall we be able, in the future, to be a member of the great international organizations which are engaged in disarmament if we are no longer interested in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization? We have allies that we must support and help, and we know also that the best defence for Canada is still that of Europe. Even if the Prime Minister would like to convince Canadians that his policy would enable taxpayers to save money, I think that if he withdrew Canadian troops to ensure a more adequate defence of our territory, Canadian taxpayers would not save anything. If air-borne forces were sent to help the members of the Alliance, I think, with figures to support me, that it would not save money to the Canadian taxpayers but that on the contrary it would entail additional expenditures.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m1
So, Mr. Speaker, I maintain that the government's decision to reduce its forces within NATO will contribute to increase the antagonism of the Warsaw Pact countries.
What struck me most after the statement of the Prime Minister of Canada regarding the review of our role within NATO was that not a single allied country congratulated the Canadian government. We have received official congratulations only from the U.S.S.R.

April 24. 1969

Now, Mr. Speaker, all hon. members know that the main enemy for Europe, Canada and the United States is still the U.S.S.R. If I were the Prime Minister of Canada, I would beware of congratulations offered me by the U.S.S.R. for a reduction of our forces in NATO.
I feel that this will not lead the Warsaw Pact countries to behave in a more conciliatory manner in dealing with the NATO countries.
Mr. Speaker, I think that this decision is untimely. The Prime Minister should heed the advice of the Minister of National Defence who is supposed to have said several times the opposite in some statements he made in public.
This decision of the government will tarnish, as I said, our international image. Canada will no longer play the role it played before, when he was chosen as mediator in conflicts that arose now and then in the world.
For all these reasons, and after hearing all the evidence during that trip, I approve straight away the amendment proposed by my party leader. In my opinion Canada should reverse the decision to reduce our forces in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
Mr. Speaker, during the last election campaign we were told about a policy of participation and I am wondering why members of the committee on external affairs and national defence were sent in Europe. We studied the problems on the spot. We gathered information. We rubbed elbows with experts and met important peoples. Upon our return, we presented immediately our report to the house and under paragraph 2 of this report we stated that Canada should continue to maintain forces in Europe according to the terms of the NATO collective defence agreements. We gave a lot of thought to this during our trip back and it was almost unanimously that we made this recommendation.
I wonder why the cabinet did not take our recommendations into account. What has become of the policy of participation of the present govermnent and particularly what is the value, the importance given to the work of our committees? When reports presented to the house, like the one concerning NATO, are put aside by the Prime Minister, it is frustrating.
Mr. Speaker, in closing I must say that the amendment moved by the leader of my party is practical and clearly reflects the present
[Mr. Asselin.i
circumstances as far as the international tension is concerned. I hope that the Liberal members who went on that trip and considered the problem of Canada's participation in NATO, will, upon thinking things over, support the amendment moved on behalf of my party, to show their disagreement with the Prime Minister's statement which is confusing and does not offer anything new in respect of the review of Canada's role in NATO.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having heard the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) speech yesterday and having given it much consideration, I respectfully submit that he has taken a bold initiative to strengthen our country's foreign policy. He has stated that no other parliament will make our foreign policy. I contrast that remark with those of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who said we have waffled, bungled and watered down our foreign policy.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
He accused the government of being isolationist. Nothing could be farther from the truth. Our -country at this time is busily engaged at Geneva at the disarmament conference. Ambassador George Ignatieff is taking a prominent part in the discussions in one of the highest councils of the world in an effort to secure world peace. He outlined to members of the committee some far-reaching, broadly visionary, and practical schemes to bring about detente. In light of that I ask, is this a government -of isolationism? I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, it is absolute poppycock to call Canadian policy isolationist.
Hon. members probably know that the external affairs committee made a report.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Where is it?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
They will also know that we visited Geneva and heard outlined a program for disarmament. That program is being negotiated at this time in the highest council of the world at Geneva. Efforts are being made by our Canadian representative. I ask, which country made an effort to bring the Warsaw Pact and NATO countries together at the conference table in order to secure detente? It was Canada. Is this the country of isolationism the Leader of the Opposition speaks of? If it is, it certainly is not the one I know and am proud to represent.
I believe our responsibilities toward NATO require a significant change. As the Prime
April 24. 1969

Minister said yesterday, we should not always be tied to heavy armour and tanks.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Nobody said that.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
We want to question NATO's present role, and to reserve the right to question it. That is what we are doing. We believe in leaving troops in NATO, but we also believe in locating them where they can be used most efficiently. At any rate, I advocate that. I believe the armoured brigade is too fixed in nature. Germany is better able to supply armour in Europe than is Canada.
Personally, I advocate a highly mobile armoured force. It should be lightly armoured but air transportable so that it can be used in Canada, Europe, or as a peacekeeping force in other areas. I think this would bring about a more practical use of our arms than has been the case in the past. Having an armoured brigade anchored to one spot and geared to staying in Europe ad infinitum, does not show much imagination. I think that the role of our forces ought to be changed significantly. As light, mobile forces they should be geared to undertaking operations anywhere in the world as peacekeeping forces.
Members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence visited Europe. We had an opportunity to examine Canada's role in1 NATO, and we began with Cyprus. It is with great pride that I report on the role Canadians are playing as part of the United Nations peacekeeping force in Cyprus. Our men are setting an example to the entire world. Do they come from a country geared to the isolationism the Leader of the Opposition speaks of? Our troops have preserved the peace in Cyprus for over two years in cooperation with other United Nations troops. I have heard predictions that, in co-operation with unarmed United Nations observers, we shall accomplish a very great step forward in peacekeeping roles under the United Nations.
On visiting France and Germany we saw that our forces were well trained, well equipped and doing a first rate job. Their morale was high. I wish to commend the way officers and men are carrying out their duties. As I said a moment ago, we saw Ambassador Ignatieff at Geneva and we also were able to capture the spirit which will lead to future disarmament. Fostering this spirit is, I believe, one of our primary roles.
In Sweden we were entertained by members of a civilized and neutral country. They were most hospitable and friendly. One must remember that Sweden is much smaller than

Canada and does not share a 3,000-mile border with the United States. Neither do they lie between the United States and Russia. While neutralism may work for Sweden, it would be an unrealistic role for Canada to adopt.
After having heard relatively harsh discussions in Paris, we were heartened at Brussels, in Belgium, to hear the brilliant and hopeful words of Mr. Harmel, foreign minister of Begium. His belief, shared by many who served on our committee, is that we should seek multilateral withdrawal of troops from Europe as a means to detente. That is No. 5 among our recommendations, and we have viewed this matter very seriously indeed. We all stand by that recommendation so far as I know. Any members that I have spoken to certainly stand by our obligation to negotiate a detente with the Warsaw Pact nations.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I personally believe that our role in NATO must always be by physical presence. Any realistic alliance requires presence of forces to demonstrate solidarity of purpose. I believe that serious discussion must continue at the highest level toward multilateral disarmament. I am distressed that the NATO-Warsaw Pact Conference seems to have bogged down in interminable technical delay. I submit we should press on with those discussions immediately. I urge a demonstration of our intention to carry out our policy of detente. I believe detente can best be achieved by conferences such as are proceeding in Geneva. I urge the government to open up discussions with the Warsaw Pact countries and NATO immediately.
In keeping with my leader and members of the committee, I do not believe we have let this country down one bit by asserting our own independence. We stand as an independent nation. We are not dominated by those in Europe or anywhere else. We are very independent. We are being led forward to assert ourselves- as an entity. I have confidence in the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux). We will maintain our genuine solidarity by keeping troops in Europe.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is puzzling to know what the main motion means. Of late it is being said that God is dead. Yesterday and today I have been thinking that whether or not that is true, surely Mackenzie King is still alive! There has been a great effort here to flutter with the

April 24, 1969

hawks and coo with the doves at the same time.
We are today examining NATO itself. We are putting that alliance under scrutiny. We must look at the effect upon us of the dimunition of our role. That is exactly what it is. We must also look at the effect of Canada adopting such a policy. NATO has always been under attack by those who are our enemies. It has always been regarded by them as a militant group, a collection of war-like nations.
We find in the arguments put forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others the suggestion that NATO has seemingly become an inhibitor to Canada in the whole field of foreign policy.
In Calgary the Prime Minister stated that NATO had become practically all of our foreign policy. He said we had no foreign policy of any importance except that which flowed from NATO. He said, "We do not want a military alliance or defence policy to pre-empt our choice." Does NATO pre-empt all our choices? Is it NATO which contributes to world tension? Is NATO deterring the detente? Is NATO a threatening alliance? Does NATO really menace eastern Europe? Would Canada be a better and more effective member of the United Nations if we were not a NATO member? Not much mention has been made of the United Nations by the Prime Minister. What would happen if we were a less active or non-member of NATO? Are we less competent in the world scene because of our membership in NATO?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) was also in Calgary. He said:
This arrangement gives smaller members of the alliance like Canada a chance to participate in the making of policy on a wide range of major issues of concern to us that we would not have in any other circumstances.
Because of our NATO membership, are we inhibited in our pursuit of peace and in our efforts to play a more meaningful role in diminishing world tension and decreasing ignorance, want and starvation? I submit to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that on the question of suffering in Biafra other members of this alliance were able to do far more than we did and the alliance did not inhibit them. Are our efforts to bridge the gulf between the haves and the have-nots, the developed and developing nations1, vitiated by our membership card in NATO? Is the NATO tag inhibiting the entrance to Peking? One of the first members to go through that door was Britain. Are we inhibited from relationships
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
with the Vatican because we are a NATO member? Hardly! Have we really been tied in such a strait-jacket by our NATO membership? Has there been anything we could have done in the world scene to follow the goal set out by the Prime Minister which we were kept from doing because of being a NATO member?
Is the dimunition of our NATO role being put forward as a means whereby a greater degree of our national budget will be allocated for other activities such as external aid? This we do not hear. Another such suggestion which has been made is that if it is not harmful to our greater and broader efforts, NATO has reached a stage where our contribution can be diminished. It has been said that Europe can defend itself. We must look at this in a thoughtful way. We are not involved in NATO to defend Europe, but in fact to defend ourselves. The Secretary of State for External Affairs in his famous Calgary speech said:
-I cannot escape the conclusion that what happens in Europe matters very much to Canada. Our interests there cover many areas-history, culture, trade and finance, to mention only a few. Perhaps the most fundamental of all, however, relates to the fact that it is in Europe that the vital interests of the superpowers are in starkest confrontation, so that there is the greatest chance of a conflict escalating into a nuclear war. Because of Canada's geographic position between the two superpowers, this war would be fought out above our very heads. This is why Canada has a direct, selfish interest in the prevention of war.
There is no suggestion there that Europe could take care of itself.

speechtext: You should have planned your time a little better.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
I do not want to be interrupted because I do not have much time. NATO by its continuing existence as an international alliance has established quite a record of longevity. It has demonstrated an emotional solidarity and common awareness of values which makes it quite a significant organization. I agree with those who believe it has done far better in military co-operation than in non-military matters. This I deplore and regret.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
This is an area in which we should give an increasingly active lead. There are questions about military obsolescence about which we
April 24, 1969

laymen do not know. I am a bit disturbed when I hear about submarine chasers whose top speed is a little slower than the submarines they are supposed to be chasing. There are questions of hardware. Of course there are. I think it would have been far more helpful in this instance if we had had a clear statement of what we are basing these decisions on. Are we withdrawing troops to save money? Are we to dismantle our military establishment and make an alternative use of this pcfttion of our national budget? This has not been said. No one should suggest that Canada is inhibited by its NATO membership from doing the things which as a highly developed and long-time, internationalist-minded, sensitive nation it should be doing to help other nations.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brew-in) has gone back to the proposal for a cadre of peacekeepers. This is an attractive suggestion, but the sad part of it is that as I look at the decisions taken in the various bodies of the United Nations there seems not to be as great an acceptance of this idea as there was originally.
There are many decisions on foreign aid which the government could have taken long ago irrespective of whether or not Canada was to remain in NATO. We have a most excellent man directing our international development agency. We have built up a good reputation in the field of foreign aid, although it is true we have made a number of bloopers, but I cannot believe that a country with our limited resources can mount a meaningful program of aid to 64 countries all over the world. Surely we should approach more effectively the matter of foreign aid without divesting ourselves of our NATO role. It is not NATO which is preventing us from being more active in that important field.
I agree with those who stress that the great crisis ahead is between those who belong to the have nations and those who belong to the have-not nations of the world. At the United Nations a few years ago I heard a great statesman say that the decisions for the next generation may very well be decided by the people who live south of the equator, whose problems at present are monumental and whose resources are so very minimal. But there are many things we should do without looking on NATO as an excuse for inaction. There is an area to our south crying out for greater aid. The former British West Indies in the Caribbean area is a place where there are grave problems. A just mixture of

Canadian interest and involvement could do wonderful things there, and perhaps make all the difference between economic and political stability and viability and something else.
I am sorry to say that this argument has been based not upon fundamentals but the suggestion that to change, to be contemporary, is somehow to be profound and to be clever. One remark I noted by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn), in a speech which impressed me as-I would not like to call it nationalistic jingoism, but if somebody else said that I do not have the argumentation to deny it-was that:
Our policies may sometimes be right; they may sometimes be wrong. But the important thing, to my mind, is that they will be made in Canada.
I say that a homemade fiasco is still a fiasco. The important thing is that these policies be made wisely and well so that they will be in Canada's interests. It is in Canada's interests not to look upon itself only, not to turn inward but to look upon its place in the world scene, to consult with its allies, to look over the opportunities and the challenges of the broad world, and not to rest upon the laurels of being novel or of being excessively nationalistic so that whatever blunders are made we can proudly say in the future that not only did we do something new in the realm of stupidity but we did it alone here in Canada.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to support the government motion because it goes in the direction I would like to go, but I want to make it clear that I do not find it completely satisfactory. Much will depend on what is meant by "early steps", and much will depend on what is meant by "planned and phased reduction." I would like "early" to mean as soon as possible, and I would like "planned and phased reduction" to mean a complete withdrawal of our forces from Europe.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced this policy on April 3 he said that the cabinet had only agreed to the following propositions, first, that Canada would remain in the NATO alliance and, second, that there would be a planned and phased reduction of Canadian forces in Europe. When he was questioned as to the extent and timing of the phased reduction he announced that these matters would be dealt with in phase two of his study. I understood by this that everything was open, including complete withdrawal. Of course I realize that this is an

April 24, 1969

optimistic interpretation and that the statement could also mean that there could be a reduction of our troops in Europe but not a complete withdrawal. According to my colleague who sits behind me and to my left, it means that Canadian forces will definitely be left in Europe but, as I say, I hope the reduction will lead to a complete withdrawal.
As a member of the External Affairs Committee I participated in the complete study of the NATO question, including the two months' study in Canada and the two weeks' study in Europe. In reply to some of the criticism that was levelled against that committee 1 wish to say that I feel the study the committee made in Europe was extremely valuable. If the Canadian government is going to spend millions of dollars in Europe through defence and external affairs, it is important that the elected representatives of the Canadian people find out how this money is being spent and why.
As a result of our studies I came to the conclusion that we should remain a member of the NATO alliance and that there should be a withdrawal of our troops from Europe. I would like to discuss both of these propositions. The Prime Minister said that our foreign policy should come first and that our military policy should follow our foreign policy objectives. I fully agree. I feel that our foreign policy objectives should be peace between nations, justice between nations, and security for nations from aggression, intervention and domination, and I believe that in pursuing those objectives we should remain in the NATO alliance.
At present in Europe there is a situation that is potentially dangerous for world peace. There is much at stake in Europe which contains the two most completely devastating armed camps in the world, the Warsaw Pact nations and the NATO troops. It is in Europe that a minor incident could easily escalate into a major war quicker than in any other place in the world.
If the confrontation is between the Warsaw Pact and NATO then Canada should be sitting at the council table within NATO to make sure that the policies of NATO are those of detente and disarmament vis-a-vis the Warsaw Pact, rather than of war. Our policy within NATO should be one leading toward detente, as the Harmel report has said and as NATO itself has said on several occasions. It should be a policy of trying to bring about disarmament and limitation of arms with the Warsaw Pact countries. I

would hope that Canada, within NATO, will continue to pursue that policy, especially now following the Czechoslovakian incident which some members of NATO seem to interpret as an opportunity for increasing our armaments in Europe. I would be opposed to that. I would hope we would not use it as an opportunity to escalate the arms race in Europe but would keep cool and try to still bring about some disarmament and some detente.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
If our policy within NATO is one of detente, then I think our military role in NATO must follow our political role. Therefore I would think the only policy for Canada in NATO consistent with a policy of detente is to withdraw our troops from Europe and earmark for NATO troops that will be stationed in Canada.
I should like to discuss the reasons for that policy. Some members who have spoken in this debate, one of whom was the Leader of the Opposition, have said they would like someone in this house to prove it is better for our security to have troops in Canada than to have troops in Europe. Well, if by withdrawing our troops from Europe we bring about a situation of detente, then that in my opinion would be protecting our security. I believe it is in the interests of our security to try to reduce the confrontation in Europe and try to bring about a detente. Therefore I think it is much more in the interests of our security to have our troops here in Canada than in Europe. I do not think it is a natural situation in peacetime for the troops of a country situated across an ocean to be placed in a country in Europe and strung along a so-called front, what would almost appear to be a wartime front.
I also feel that we in Canada with our limited resources are trying to play too many roles. We are not a large country. We are a country of approximately 20 million people. Yet, we find our forces in five areas of the world. We find them within Canada playing a possible defence role. We have troops stationed here for several purposes. We play a military role in the Atlantic and we play a military role in the Pacific with the Pacific arm of our navy. We are playing a peacekeeping role in the United Nations and we have troops in Europe. I have not mentioned the fact that we also have an Arctic Ocean frontier.
April 24, 1969

Many people, especially those in Europe, who look at Canada think of Canada as only an Atlantic nation. It is not. We have ties with Europe and look toward the Atlantic and Europe, but we are also a Pacific nation. We are also a very large nation in territory and yet we have a sparse population. So I feel that if we are to make the best use of our resources for defence and security we must have a specialized role. I see that specialized role as one where we have armed forces stationed in Canada which would be of a nature that they could be used for Canadian purposes, for United Nations peacekeeping purposes and for NATO purposes, but stationed in Canada and earmarked for NATO to be used in an emergency.
Some members who have spoken during this debate have spoken as if our withdrawal of troops from Europe meant a withdrawal from the military role altogether. Several Conservative members have said that this afternoon. Either they have not read the motion or they have not been listening to the debate. Nobody on this side has suggested we should completely withdraw our troops from NATO. Many countries which are members of NATO do not have troops along the east-west German frontier, but they still have a military commitment to NATO. The North Atlantic Treaty does not say that members of NATO must keep troops in Europe. It says that if one of the countries of NATO is attacked the other countries must come to its assistance, all subject to the U.N. charter. As pointed out by the Prime Minister, many countries which are members of NATO have their troops on their own soil playing a home defence role but also earmarked for NATO. When we joined NATO we did not have any troops in Europe. We sent them to Europe only during the Korean war period.
One of the arguments against a policy of keeping troops in Canada rather than in Europe is that there will be a re-emergence of German militarism. It was suggested that with the withdrawal of our troops the gap would have to be filled by the German army. When I was in Europe with the committee we met many German politicians, prominent journalists and military people. I must say that I was greatly impressed by the democratic attitude of the Germans. I personally do not feel that the majority of the people of Germany today have any sympathy whatsoever with militarism or nationalism. I get the impression they are bending the other way. If they are to be our allies I think we must not

be ambivalent in our attitude toward them. If they are to be our allies I believe we should trust them and let them play a role with us in the alliance that is suitable in relation to their size and so on. I do not suggest that they should have nuclear arms or that any other country in the alliance should have nuclear arms. I feel, however, that it is a red herring to bring into the argument a suggestion that we should not withdraw our troops from Europe because this will in some way encourage German militarism.
Second, there is the argument that if we did withdraw our troops from Europe we would not be paying our way or pulling our full load. Again I think this argument fails to recognize the fact that in withdrawing our troops from Europe we would still be earmarking troops for NATO but they would be stationed in Canada. We would be doing the same thing that is being done by many other countries in NATO which are not accused of not paying their way or not pulling their share of the load. I must point out that when people make that type of argument they do not realize that Canada, after all, is a NATO country and that Canadian territory is NATO territory. By keeping our troops in Canada and earmarking them for emergencies we are contributing to NATO and paying our way. As a matter of fact, right now and in the past few years I think we have been paying too much to NATO.
I should like to spend a few minutes discussing some of the arguments raised by other hon. members. I found the speech of the Leader of the Opposition very disappointing. He spoke for approximately 40 minutes and spent the whole time in a negative way attacking the speech made by the Prime Minister. He did not put forward an alternative proposal to that put forward by the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, owing to the time one has, I can only deal with one or two points. I want to say at the outset that I find the announced government policy on NATO to be an unhealthy compromise resulting from a lack of will to do precisely what the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) orated about yesterday, namely, to deal with the world of today and refuse to be bound by the actions of yesterday. I also say before I go any farther, and this follows the position our leader expressed yesterday along with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), that we cannot vote for the Conservative amendment because, despite its wording which was rather original, obviously what the Conservatives want is the status quo for Canada in NATO and, indeed, to strengthen our military contribution. We do not agree with this and will therefore vote against the amendment.
On April 13 when the Prime Minister first announced his so-called policy, and I have to say that because I do not yet know what it is, I said at a press conference in the absence of my leader that the Prime Minister's statement made that day was imprecise and confusing. That still remains true. His excuse appears to be that he has not yet completed the review of our foreign and defence policies. First, I cannot understand that or why it should take so long in view of the immense resources at the disposal of the government. In any case I would say, without intending to be offensive but very sincerely and firmly, that if the Prime Minister has not yet decided on his policies then he should stop talking as if he had. If he has nothing to tell parliament or the people of Canada he should say so instead of indulging in general lectures which merely add to confusion at home and to uncertainty abroad.
[Mr. Allmand.l
If the Prime Minister's statement means anything at all in so far as one can gather what it means, then his analysis leads to the clear and inevitable conclusion that Canada should withdraw all its forces from Europe as quickly as possible after consultation with its allies. Why do I say that? Time and again the Prime Minister at his press conference on April 3, in his speech on April 12 in Calgary, and in speech yesterday, emphasized that our military contribution in Europe is marginal that it is insubstantial and that our proper role in NATO is political rather than military. We agree with all of that and I agree with him also that the situation in western Europe has changed. When NATO was first established that part of the world was economically devastated and militarily dismantled. Today, fortunately, western Europe is economically and, therefore, militarily strong. The Prime Minister said this on more than one occasion and we agree with him in this analysis.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the Prime Minister had the courage of his convictions then the clear and inescapable conclusion from this analysis would be that Canada's forces in Europe serve no useful purpose and ought to be totally withdrawn. Instead of this unequivocal policy which the N.D.P. has proposed for a few years, and proposes now, we get from the government vague words about planned and phased reduction of our forces without being told when that reduction will take place, what the size of the reduction will be and at what point it will stop.
What is even more important, as far as I am concerned, is that I simply cannot follow the logic of a government which states that a mechanized brigade and six air squadrons in Europe provide no useful role but that a smaller commitment in Europe would. This is the kind of lack of logic which makes me question the integrity of the proposition that has been pushed on this parliament and the people of Canada.
I was a member of the external affairs committee and travelled through Europe. Every one of us got the impression that I suppose his predilections led him to receive. My experience from meeting with NATO military leaders all over Europe raised a very deep concern about that organization. It led me to the conclusion which I had been gradually working toward, but it emphasized an underlying conviction that NATO has become almost entirely a powerful military alliance.
April 24, 1969

What is worse, when you speak to the leaders of NATO you get the impression, at least I did, that it is almost entirely controlled by military objectives and psychology and that it is under the domination of military leaders. The political role of NATO, I suggest, has become minimal, but lip service continues to be paid to it with no effective steps being taken to seek detente in Europe. Nor has Canada taken any steps in NATO to seek such detente. Indeed, when a while ago the Warsaw Pact issued a direct invitation to meet with the NATO powers to discuss questions of a possible political solution and a reduction of forces in Europe, what did NATO do, with the participation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux)? NATO rejected that invitation.

though smaller complexes in other countries, is in tact in control of NATO, as it is of other aspects of international and national policies, unfortunately.
I have, therefore, reached the conclusion that the time has come for a country like Canada to use its resources primarily to help raise the level of life in the developing nations, in the knowledge that the elimination of poverty and disease, lifting peoples who are now underdeveloped to a decent level of life, is an essential deterrent against war, an even more essential one than military confrontation. The time has come when Canada should use its resources in this way, rather than wasting them on military commitments of doubtful value, as the Prime Minister himself admits our commitment in Europe is. I suggest-and there is nothing original about this-that the time has come, and is in fact long overdue, when Canada should join with other, smaller countries in a relentless attack upon the insanity of the nuclear terror and on the international military-industrial complex which feeds it.
I suggest there are two facts in the modern world which any viable foreign and defence policy of a country like Canada-I am speaking only of our country-must take into account. The first is that the peace of the world now depends on the insane balance of nuclear terror, a balance that can at any moment be upset, either deliberately by some evil government or by accident by some stupid general. To rely upon the balance of nuclear terror seems to me to ask for the kind of destruction that all of us tremble may some time happen. Therefore in this case a country like Canada, without nuclear capability, not wishing to have any nuclear capability, ought in my opinion to give an immense amount of its resources, an immense amount of its energies, to every aspect of peace and disarmament negotiations in every part of the world. We should do more than that. We should speak out firmly and loudly against the continuing nuclear arms race. We should not be timid about telling Washington that we disapprove of the deployment of A.B.M.'s because they are a danger to the future peace of the world. We should do that.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: What about Russia?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
We should do that with Moscow, too, and every other military power. We should be one of the countries shouting against this kind of behaviour in the world. I am not naive enough to think that merely Canada saying it will produce results, but I

believe in something else and, if it is not true, there is no hope for the world. I believe that if a sufficient number of nations like Canada keep demanding that this insane nuclear arms race cease, if we all do it, if we all leave the military alliances so that no one can point the finger of satellite at us, as they can now, if a great enough number of countries make these demands and co-operate together to do so, at the United Nations and every other forum, eventually the sanity of the world's people will prevail. If this is not possible, there is no hope for the world.
The second major issue before the world is the question of hunger throughout the world and the danger this represents to the peace of the world. We ought to give a great deal of our resources and energies to this sphere of activity, to save and lift up the peoples of the world.
