subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to say a few words on the world situation, on NATO and on the present economic situation in Canada.
I believe it would be a good idea to give my speech the title: cannons at the expense of bread and Canadian lives. We must first establish peace amongst ourselves in Canada in order to ensure at the same time our security.
At the time present, we are faced with a rather complex international and national situation, as much for the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), as for the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux), for they must take sides and determine the nation's future, as well as the form of our participation in NATO.
Mr. Speaker, we have to remember, as was said by the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas), that for the past 20 years we have contributed to the NATO forces and when we decided to follow that course it was for a major reason but on a temporary basis only. However the years have passed and this contribution continues.
I think the time has come to put an end to it.
The government should withdraw for two years all its troops from NATO and affect instead the money spent on defence to stimulate the Canadian economy, by building houses for the Canadian people who live in slums and pay rents of $200 or $300 a month which they cannot afford.
April 24, 1969

This- is, Mr. Speaker, the humanitarian work we could do. The huge amounts spent on defence could be affected to building houses for the Canadian people, to develop industries with a view to providing work for Canadians. We could then two years later if necessary resume our participation to NATO.
But a pause of two years would enable the Canadian people to stabilize their economy because they are always faced with debts and outstanding taxes, and have to live in constant uncertainty only to pay off war debts or to contribute to some international defence system which might never be used.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that so much progress should enable us to provide our people and the destitute in other countries with the things that are essential to the well-being of man. Since we are called upon to live in a society where affluence and poverty exist side by side, our first duty, it seems to me, is to secure peace at home.
In the face of atomic war threats, there is no more urgent task than to ensure the protection of humanity. Rulers and ordinary citizens are all in the same boat, and if we are unable to find an effective means of securing peace, we are doomed to certain destruction.
In the face of all those nuclear arms and destruction hardware, we cannot afford to keep on maintaining our armed forces, which will be powerless against such tremendous weapons.
Mr. Speaker, people must put order and justice in their daily life, which is not what we are doing at present. We certainly do not put this principle into practice when we introduce bills such as the omnibus bill.
The solution to our problem is to live as men, to respect our fellowmen and to give every individual the opportunity to grow and to develop his personality.
Mr. Speaker, NATO forces should be reinforced, according to some people, under the pretext of fighting communism. But we are not even able to solve the problems of hunger and slums at home; yet, those are situations likely to promote communism. It is not with defence, or arms, or cold war that we shall fight communism.
With all our resources, our human capital, our monetary capital, our technology and our scientific research, we should be able to face communism.
Mr. Speaker, even if we are decided to do all that, we must be fully aware that it is only a materialistic force which will be used

to contain communism for some time through strength and violence, but we shall never succeed by those sole means in ensuring order, justice and peace.
If we only set might against might and counterbalance ideology, we will never beat the communist world. Neither could we do so through fear or violence, in this atomic age.
We would only destroy ourselves because our system of debts and taxes, even with Canada's 21 million people and inexhaustible resources and with the help of American technology and increased aid. Our tremendous national debt paralyses our productive activities, our purchasing power and the development of our productivity.
We can no longer produce because industries are unable to borrow money at 10 per cent or even at 24 per cent.
If we increase our expenditures for defence and armaments in proportion to our responsibilities the government will have to increase taxes, when our debt is so high that owners have to sell their homes to pay taxes and the tribute to a few individuals who control the economic life of this country.
Without regard for human beings who have the right to live, all our initiatives are affected by the same cancer eating away the honest comfort of the people, in Canada as well as in Europe and in other parts of the world.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The same system is found everywhere, but with a few variations. We could, if we wanted to, make use of all our human and physical resources and continue to expand both our respective and our common means of defence.
We could also intensify research in all sectors and increase production in all fields, thus creating jobs for the unemployed who consider themselves as useless members of society and who live in insecurity, hardship and poverty. Those people form too large a part of our population.
The situation could be improved, provided we are determined to deal with the problems, instead of letting them grow until a war comes along to upset everything.
Technical problems call for technical remedies. That is why, Mr. Speaker, we are unable to find any solutions.
Hitler proved to us that war was not only a question of money, but a question of weapons and material. Germany did not lose the war because it lacked money, but because of a shortage of troops and material.

April 24, 1969

During the war, money was flowing freely all over the world. It was then a case of killing, slaughtering, destroying. However, when the war came to an end, the monetary problems and the European problems emerged once again. Development is only possible through borrowing, being loaded with debt, at extremely high interest rates. The rates varied from 2 to 3 per cent during the war. They have now reached 7, 9 and 10 per cent.
As far as the building of houses is concerned, we should consider the things I have just said. That is where the shoe pinches, that is what causes so much misery and so much worries to humanity in the sullied history which is ours. We could manage to find a solution for a good many of our problems by making financially possible what is physically possible, in every country, in accordance with their resources in manpower and material.
Mr. Speaker, in order to give my ideas a more concrete form, I would like the House to study a resolution regarding economy and finance. We are dealing with war and defence, and not of financial matters. We shall levy taxes, we shall overtax people-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the North Atlantic Treaty story goes back to the end of world war II. The western allies, demobilized and disarmed, determined to reconstruct and rebuild. Russia, with her forces intact, embarked on a program of expansion in Europe through communist subversion. By 1948 Berlin was blockaded and free Czechoslovakia fell to Soviet expansion. It is well to remind ourselves of these things. The western nations decided it was time to say to the communists: "Thus far-no farther." This required the organization of a collective defence system which could provide a credible shield for the entire Atlantic area. Thus the North Atlantic Treaty came to being and NATO was born. This was in 1949, just 20 years ago.
During the 20-year interval the people of Western Europe have enjoyed peace and prosperity. Why has this been so? The NATO-created balance of forces and a mutual determination to resist have prevented any further communist gains in Europe. As long as the Soviet Union shows no sign of reducing her forces, this balance must be maintained. The people of Europe understand these things

very well, even though some in Canada do not. We who were with the defence committee in Europe recognized this attitude in every country we visited; it was reflected by everyone we spoke with.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: How did you know?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
I am referring to those who talked with us even though some of us may not have understood what they were saying.
It is strange that neither the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) nor any of the speakers on the government side have mentioned Czechoslovakia in this debate though in every country we visited every official to whom we spoke emphasized the events of last August when talking to us. Not one member on the other side has pointed out that the Warsaw Pact countries have continued a heavy military build-up.
The statistics are evidence of this situation. The combined strength of the Warsaw Pact countries in direct confrontation with the west is 170 divisions of ground forces with 7,000 aircraft. Combined NATO forces total 76 divisions and only 3,200 aircraft. In the central European sector where the Canadian forces are deployed the picture is even more lopsided. There are 100 ground divisions on the Warsaw Pact side with 3,400 aircraft. On the combined NATO side there are 26 divisions and 2,000 planes. These are the statistics lor last year.
I come now to a further point, and I have not heard any member on the government side mention this either. Last year NATO reduced its forces by 80,000 troops. If the Warsaw Pact countries had any intention to de-escalate they would have decreased their forces in like number, as it was expected they might do because an attitude of detente was present in Europe. But this did not happen. Instead, the Warsaw Pact countries invaded Czechoslovakia.
Consider the case of Norway. At the time of joining NATO Norway required that no foreign troops should be located on its soil and that no nuclear arms should be placed there. With such a policy one might expect that the U.S.S.R. would place a lesser force on its common border with Norway than in other parts of Europe. But this has not been the case. There has been a continued build-up along this northern frontier as well.
It is obvious that Soviet policy regarding NATO is clear and simple: first, to weaken the will of individual NATO members to resist and, second, to split NATO into its
April 24, 1969

European and United States components. I contend this is what the Prime Minister is bringing to pass with the policy he has now enunciated. We hear continued talk from some members of the government party and of the N.D.P. about the United States industrial-military complex. But I say that the industrial-military complex in the United States is ruled by a democratic government. Those same hon. members say nothing about the industrial-military complex in Russia where it is not ruled by a democratic process but rather where it is a law unto itself.
We need to remind ourselves that Khrushchev no longer rules in the Kremlin. The present rulers of the Kremlin are all older men trained under Stalin, men who have obviously reverted to a Stalinistic policy which, under Khrushchev, had perhaps begun to change. There is no evidence in modern history that the communists have ever been ready to talk in face of weakness. On the other hand, that there is plenty of evidence that they do talk in face of strength. What happened in Czechoslovakia is clear evidence that the Soviets will use brute force whenever they can get away with it. This is why the conventional role of military equipment has not yet seen its day in Europe. The Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia. The NATO alliance is just as necessary today on the military side as it was in 1949.
We are asked now to accept the views of a man who has been entrusted with the great responsibility of the office of Prime Minister but who holds a pre-conceived idea of the world based on a doctrinaire ideology that the U.S.S.R. is mellowing, that there is no longer any danger of confrontation. Well, Mr. Speaker, the United Kingdom minister of defence told the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence that this was an ideological perch. He urged that the committee come down from that ideological perch and face the facts.
The Hon. Mr. Denis Healey said that the practical reality of life was that the basis of security and peace in Europe still depended upon a strong NATO. The day might come, he added, when de-escalation of the military aspect would be possible, and Britain would welcome it when it came, but under the present leadership and policies of the U.S.S.R. it was not yet a reality.
I would remind members of the New Democratic party, including the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), that the

labour-socialist government in the United Kingdom, which they claim to be a party similar to their own, made it very clear that the policy advocated by the N.D.P. in this country was wrong. Today Britain is increasing its commitment to NATO in response to the situation which exists at the present time.
The Prime Minister said yesterday that those who criticize his policy as being isolationist have a fixation on old wars and old problems. I say to the Prime Minister that he is altogether wrong in this assumption. It is he who lives in a dream world, refusing to face the facts of life in 1969. His philosophy is not new. He promulgated it when he was part of the Peace Research Institute a few years ago. Chamberlain did the same in 1938. The only people he pleases are the bitter isolationists in the United States and those who smirk behind the curtains. Certainly he is not pleasing the Canadian people.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
On December 1, 1968, the Canadian Institute of Public Opinion revealed that 64 per cent of the Canadian people believed that Canadian troops should continue to stay in Europe as part of the NATO forces. No wonder the government is split on this issue. The consensus of government members on the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence was that we should continue to play our part in NATO. This difference of opinion caused Senator Aird to resign. He refused to accept the kind of policies being advocated at present. No wonder the government is split in this regard.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I sympathize with the Prime Minister. For one who took the position during world war II that the war was being fought between the imperialists and had nothing to do with Canada, and who in the years following world war II took another, well known position it must now be extremely difficult to enunciate a realistic defence policy. I do not believe the leader of our nation has the right to formulate a minority policy which would mean a breaking away of Canadian foreign policy from that of our friends and allies. Neither has he the right to discuss and formulate defence policies which are out of context with what is going on today in the world.
The Prime Minister talked about Canada withdrawing to a continental role and of his hope that Canada will lead in the field of disarmament research. I ask, what has the 17-nation United Nations commission on

April 24, 1969

disarmament been doing for the past ten years? Those 17 nations, of which Canada is one, have done a commendable job. Has that commission succeeded? No, it has not. I remind the Prime Minister that the secret of disarmament will be found in the willingness of the U.S.S.R. to agree to disarmament. It is as simple as that, and the representatives of the 17 nations on the commission know it.
Recently the members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence visited four NATO countries in Europe, one neutral nation and one non-aligned nation. Without exception all those nations did not want Canada to weaken NATO by withdrawing from it. Neither did our senior diplomatic and military personnel serving in Europe, who are authorities on this subject, wish us to withdraw.
It is interesting to note that Canada's defence budget, when it is related to gross national product, is far lower than that of any other NATO country. When he appeared before our committee the foreign minister of Belgium was asked what he thought of the possibility of Canada withdrawing in whole or in part from NATO. He answered quickly by saying: "Such action is incredible. We smaller nations need and must have the support of a larger middle power such as Canada, free and freedom loving." The statesmen of Europe said that the purpose of NATO is to keep the peace in Europe. It is to prevent hell in Europe and not to create heaven.
I submit that the purpose of NATO in part is to give the smaller nations a collective power and force which without NATO they would not have. They must have that force and influence both within and without NATO. This applies not only to the military role of NATO but also to the economic, political and cultural aspects as well. May I also point out that NATO has a secondary function, that of keeping the balance of power in Europe. Here I refer to the fact that as part of NATO Germany is a lesser threat to Russia or to anyone else than she would be if she were on her own and out of NATO.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that Canada's role in NATO is a positive one. It is a morale-building role. We uphold the morale of the smaller nations of the Atlantic community. The purpose of NATO also is to bring about strength through collective security. It is to strengthen neighbours and friends who are part of the Atlantic community. Above all, Mr. Speaker, NATO is a peacekeeping force. In fact, when we participate in

NATO we participate in the most important peacekeeping role there is today in the world.
It is inevitable that this situation will change, and I hope it will change for the better. I hope that when changes come we shall be able to adapt to them. In the meantime our role in NATO must continue as at present, I also hope that our role on the economic, political and cultural planes will be enlarged. At present, however, reality demands that we should remain in NATO and that we should make our military contribution in Europe. Any new role to be undertaken ought to be worked out in co-operation with our NATO allies. There is no other way for us to act.

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Minister of National Defence):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak after my good friend from Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) in this debate, because he has just stated, I believe, that after all he fully supports the policy advocated by the government. In fact, he has just said that we must keep our membership in NATO and that we must make a realistic contribution in Europe. This is precisely the significance of the governmental policy.
My friend, the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin), referred a while ago to the various statements which I have already made in this connection. I do not know if he was trying to embarrass me, but if so, he failed, because in the past I have said two things, among others, namely that I considered NATO as being essential to the security of Canada and that it had a part to play in addition to its military role.
Now, after extensive studies by the ministerial committee, we have in the first place rejected any suggestion leading to the neutrality of Canada. In the second place, we have stated that we adhered to the principles of collective security and thirdly, that we were going to maintain our membership in NATO. Consequently, I do not see why the position of the government could in any way embarrass me now, as a result of my previous statements.
Mr. Speaker, I have also stated on several occasions that, in my opinion, those defence matters should also seek both a detente and disarmament.
Unlike my good friend from York South, I am convinced that the Atlantic Alliance has made some valid efforts which furthermore have already proved successful.
April 24, 1969



For example, he raised the matter of the Budapest communique, and he said that Canada had never taken any initiative towards a detente, and that we had advised to reject the proposal from the Warsaw group.
I would remind him that the communique of the meeting in Washington insisted precisely on the fact that the participating nations had asked that the proposal be examined carefully and that there be efforts made to overcome the obstacles which, at first sight, seemed to prevent us from initiating the necessary negotiations right now.
We have also indicated that the discussions on the Budapest communique resulted from a Canadian paper on East-West relations. Therefore, I sincerely believe, Mr. Speaker, that to the extent that such action can be effective, Canada has already made a useful contribution to the cause of disarmament through NATO.
At the time my good friend opposite was Minister of National Defence, our participation to NATO was reduced as it was last year or this year, when I announced that we had to close the Zweibriicken base. The opposition did not blame us, because it was a realistic decision. By concentrating our forces in two bases, we were able to save money in the fields of administration and staff.
It was said also that no government member reacted when Czechoslovakia was invaded. Has it been forgotten, for example, that our reaction was to delay the decision to make a 20 per cent reduction in our air forces? That was how the Canadian government reacted to the invasion of Czechoslovakia.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have now reached phase 2 of this long-term study, as was announced by the Prime Minister. It is now up to the Minister and to the Department of National Defence to translate the government's decision into military and realistic terms.

The purpose of this phase is to determine the kinds of forces and equipment best suited
to carry out the military roles to meet defence policy objectives outlined in the statement of principle issued by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on April 3, 1969. It is a military planning phase. It involves detailed military plans and since a change in the operation of a complex force, is also involved, some hon. members will appreciate that considerable time inevitably will be taken before it is completed. In this process, we will be considering, inter alia, a number of alternative plans for the reduction of our forces stationed in Europe, and what type of forces we should continue to maintain to enable us to contribute effectively to collective security abroad.
In his statement yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said that Canada's resources, although immense, are not limitless. Let me add, sir, that the share of these resources at the disposition of the government also is not limitless, and that defence is one of many competing demands made upon these resources. Amongst the objectives of the government's defence policy outlined in the statement issued by the Prime Minister on April 3, there are two which I wish to emphasize.
First, that our forces will be capable of playing important roles in collective security and peace keeping. This, sir, is not an isolationist or fortress America objective. Second, that the structure, equipment and training of our forces must be compatible with their performance of the four roles: the surveillance of our territory, the defence of North America, support of NATO, and international peace keeping. Ini their present roles, our forces committed to NATO require different equipment and different training from the forces we maintain in Canada for national purposes and to carry out international peace keeping missions. The differences or incompatibilities in maintaining two different kinds of forces increase our defence costs and, if continued in the future, would increase them even more.
An objective of our current studies is, therefore, to develop in the next few years fully compatible forces, which will provide at the same time a capacity to play important roles in collective security and peace keeping. Unless all are prepared to accept a large increase in our defence expenditures, the present roles of our forces now in Europe limit our ability to achieve the posture for the Canadian forces which the government believes appropriate for the future. To overcome this, we must start now to convert our

April 24, 1969

forces from their present roles in Europe and to plan the reduction of the total number of Canadian forces which are stationed there. The size and timing of these reductions remains to be decided when our planning is completed.
We have said all along that all this would be done in consultation with our allies. I do not see where we differ with the members on the other side on this particular point. The government has stated that it will begin consultations with our NATO allies on our proposals for the planned and phased reduction of the Canadian forces stationed in Europe at the ministerial meeting of the NATO Defence Planning Committee, which is to be held at the end of May of this year.
The normal procedure used by the NATO member nations to consult with each other regarding any changes which they plan to make in their forces assigned or earmarked for assignment to the integrated NATO commands, such as the Allied Command in Europe or the Allied Command Atlantic, is the NATO defence planning review. The May meeting of the Defence Planning Committee will initiate a new cycle in the NATO defence planning review, which for the first time will be carried out over a period of two years.
The main task of the defence ministers at this meeting will be to decide, in the light of an appreciation of the military situation to be presented by the NATO military authorities, what guidance, political, economic and financial, should be given to the NATO military planners as the basis for their preparation of the over-all NATO force plans for the years 1971 to 1975, inclusive. The major NATO commanders and the NATO military committee will develop their force plans in the light of the guidance provided by the ministers. Again, I refer to some of the remarks that this is entirely a military organization controlled by generals. This is not so. The political direction is clearly indicated in that procedure.
NATO force planning must take into account the military plans of the member nations, and I think it only reasonable, at the beginning of a new NATO planning cycle, that Canada should provide its allies and the NATO military staffs with as much indication of its planning intentions as is possible. It is my expectation, Mr. Speaker, that phase II of our defence policy review will have advanced sufficiently by the end of May, that I shall be able to present to my NATO colleagues a fairly detailed outline of that part of our

force plans affecting our present NATO undertakings.
Hon. members will be aware that national undertakings to commit forces to the NATO commands are given for a period of one year. Our present undertakings extend to the end of 1969. As a part of the NATO defence planning review running separately from, but in parallel with, the development of the over-all force plans for the years 1971-75, we shall be asked during the next few months to inform NATO what forces we plan to commit to the NATO commands during the year 1970. Our plans for this one year will be reviewed with the NATO military authorities and our allies in the fall and we shall be asked to adopt them as firm commitments until the end of 1970 at the ministerial meeting in December. I trust that this explanation will clear any misunderstandings that have recently come to light.
As the house will know, Mr. Speaker, well established procedures exist, through the Permanent Joint Board on Defence and other bodies, for continuing consultation with our United States allies on matters affecting our joint efforts in the defence of North America. As the plans to implement our new policy take shape, we shall be using these procedures to discuss with the United States government how we can best contribute in future to the defence of the continent. Joint studies have already begun on the plan for modernization of the system of bomber defence. We shall be able to decide how we can most usefully contribute both to the surveillance of our air space and to the modernized antibomber system as those studies proceed. We shall also be seeking early occasions to consult the United States government as to how we can employ the maritime and land forces which we require for our national purposes to the best advantage in furthering our mutual interests in defending the continent.
As hon. members will understand, this period of planning and consultation will take some time. No doubt during this time there will be conjecture as to what we plan to do. As Minister of National Defence, I am concerned that these conjectures will have an upsetting effect on the members of our forces. We, as members of parliament awaiting the results on election night, can understand the feelings of the forces during this period.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It will be a difficult period during which time a number of changes will be discussed
April 24, 1969

and examined by the Defence Staff. Some of these plans will be incorporated into the over-all plan and others will be discarded. I want to assure hon. members, and especially I want to assure all of the members of the Canadian Armed Forces, that our plans will not be announced until we feel confident that every option has been fully analysed by itself and in relation to other options. I want to repeat to the forces that conjecture will be simply conjecture.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members will agree that defence problems never remain static. The members of the Canadian Armed Forces have demonstratively proved that they are ready and able to adapt to any new change, perhaps more than any other segment of our society. The Canadian Armed Forces must continually make readjustments to meet changing defence problems. As hon. members are well aware, the members of the Canadian Armed Forces have been undergoing a change towards unification for the past few years. It has not been an easy task, but their professionalism and sense of duty have overcome many of the obstacles.
Now, we must undertake new tasks to meet the new policy roles. How these tasks will be carried out, as I said before, is being examined by the Defence Staff. I am sure that we can expect the continued high degree of professionalism from the forces that they have so ably demonstrated in the past. In return, I think every Canadian should, by whatever means he can, recognize that our forces have made many sacrifices in the past and have endured many hardships in the performance of their duty. This is a part of their life which they are willing to accept, providing the objectives are clear and sensible.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks, following immediately upon the comments of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux), will be a little bit disjointed. I would like to make some comments on the minister's explanations', but in the absence of a text it is difficult to bring the whole thing into clear focus. I hope that later this evening someone will have an opportunity to deal with one or two points that the minister attempted to clarify, but about which questions1 were left dangling as a result of his explanations. The matter raised with him by direct question just a moment ago is one of them.
In the context of any defence review, it is difficult to ignore what is topical and of major concern. Here, I refer to the A.B.M. system. It is a matter of understandable regret that the minister was not able to deal with it. It is also a matter of regret that he was not able to give us more specific information, particularly from the standpoint of those who are serving in our armed forces. As long as questions such as this remain' unanswered there will be uncertainty and fear in the minds of officers and men, not only among those serving in continental Europe but also those serving in Canada.
I join with everybody else who has said that we would welcome a proper opportunity to get out of the business of war, out of anything that has to do with war, so that we could) bring our troops home from Europe. As a matter of fact in that context, we would even welcome the disbandonment of Maritime Command, but I caution the minister in any review he undertakes not to lay a finger on it.
I intend to restrict my remarks to the report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. That report

April 24. 1969

represents several months of concentrated effort on the part of 30 men, not to mention 16 eminent witnesses from the academic and other fields in Canada and from as far away as Germany.
I think the questions and the arguments that developed were sound. The witnesses placed well thought out positions before the committee and these were deeply considered by members of the committee. The headings in the report are indicative of the extent to which witnesses and members went in trying to arrive at some rational conclusion on what Canada's defence posture should be in relation to NATO.
The committee dealt briefly with Canada's membership in the United Nations. We indicated to this house and to the country that we did not feel Canada was directly menaced by any threat of invasion, and that the threat to Canada lay elsewhere, primarily in Europe. We reviewed our existing alliances. I hope that the Minister of National Defence will include these in his review because I doubt if there is a living Canadian who can recite all 47 of them.
We dealt with NATO, with its history and its provisions. We were all very much aware of the role that Canada had to play within the terms of that alliance. We were all aware that we were not committed to send troops to Europe. We touched on NORAD and indicated to the people of Canada that members of the committee had not agreed on any definitive roles in this context. We felt the committee should go further into this matter in the near future. Our present military contribution to NATO was thoroughly reviewed, both here at home and by a physical tour of Europe.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
We dealt with the question of neutrality for Canada. I might say I was pleased to see the government's rejection of this as an optional role for Canada at this particular time. I am one of those who has long believed we cannot afford the luxury of neutrality. We went on to deal with the question of whether or not Canada should rely on the United States for its sole protection. Here, we get closer to the matters with which I should like to deal. The presentations made before the committee in some part-not in whole because there was considerable opposition to this-argued that Canada could substantially reduce the amount of money presently being spent on defence because the geographic proximity of the United States makes it necessary for the
[Mr. Forrestall.l
United States, in a sense, to defend Canada in order to defend itself. This was referred to I think as the so-called "free ride" theory. These arguments were rejected by the committee. Quite to the contrary, there is a conviction among all members of the committee I am sure, and among most Canadians with whom I have had an opportunity to discuss this, that Canada should be prepared to incur its fair and reasonable share of military responsibility in the world. Particularly, we must be prepared to do that and indeed are prepared to do that, so far as our relations with the United States are concerned.
The question of foreign aid being substituted for defence expenditures was rejected by the committee. I indicate to the minister, as he is probably well aware, that this is a question the committee probably will want to examine in some depth at a very early opportunity. The question of our peacekeeping role has been dealt with. In this connection the minister surely is well aware, much more so than the members of the committee, of the difficulty in pursuing this as a primary line of defence posture for Canada.
This leads us to the impact of the effect of Canada's alliance membership, not only our political affiliation but our full role within our means within the integrated military structure of NATO. In our report at page 35, the second last paragraph, there is this conclusion:
*-Canada's influence with other nations of the world, including the non-aligned and developing nations-
The so-called third world.
-will be determined more by the degree of independence, objectivity and fairness which Canada exhibits in its relations with other countries than by its alliance associations.
My dear friend from Hillsborough posed a number of questions which I think are valid. I would repeat one of them. He asked in what way does our association with NATO and NATO's- integrated military structure inhibit those- things that the so-called doves would pursue with eagerness and ait the expense of Canada making a fair and equitable contribution to the defence of the western world. I fail to see any way. I fail to see any real argument that we should not bear the cost of maintaining a physical presence in Europe. At -least I fail to see one that would persuade any individual who has bothered to look into the question-.
Indeed, it is my understanding the cost of keeping our troops in Europe is approximately $20 million. I am perfectly aware that the
April 24. 1969

paper figures run somewhere in the order of $140 million. In the absence of a clearly enunciated policy in respect of what we would do with these troops when we bring them home, that is whether they would be employed in the surveillance of our territory and whether or not maritime command might form the basis for a specialized military role, and ini the absence of any indication that we would substantially expand our air capability here in North America or our ground troops, I can only conclude that it is premature to seriously consider even a phased reduction. I think we all know a phased reduction will mean a total reduction.
To those who have supported the government motion in the hope that a phased plan of reduction will mean the withdrawal from NATO of only a few troops, I say they are whistling in the dark. They know very well, as do all of us, that once reduction starts, phased or otherwise, it will be total. If the Minister of National Defence remains in that capacity I predict he will find shortly after August, the first point at which we can indicate to our partners in the Alliance that we intend to withdraw in one year's time, that it will be a sorry day for Canada and its integrity among not only the western nations of the world but among all the countries of the world.
